### Quantification and statistical analysis

#### Data analysis

Behavioural data were analysed in R (https://www.r-project.org/, version 2022.07.0) using the packages dplyr, tidyr, ggplot2, ez, wesanderson, lme4, reshape2, readxl, rstatix, and RColorBrewer. For the analysis of the EEG data, we used the MATLAB toolboxes EEGLAB (http://sccn.ucsd.edu/eeglab/, version, version 14.1.2b) and fieldtrip (https://www.fieldtriptoolbox.org/, version 20190819) as well as custom made scripts. The error probability of 5% was chosen for all statistical tests. Where appropriate, we corrected the p-values for false discovery rate in multiple hypothesis testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg method.

#### Behavioural data analysis

The outcome measure for sleep-learning was wake-retrieval accuracy at 12 hr and at 36 hr. Participants assigned the previously sleep-played and new pseudowords to one of three categories (animal, tool, place). If the assigned category corresponded to the superordinate category of the translation word that had been played during sleep along with the pseudoword, then the participant’s response was classified as correct. Participants’ assignments of new pseudowords to the three categories were neither correct nor incorrect because new pseudowords were not associated with a certain translation word. The new pseudowords were included at the 12 hr and the 36 hr retrieval as a baseline for the event-related EEG potential analyses (correct versus incorrect versus baseline).

Categorization accuracy for previously sleep-played pseudowords was expressed as percentage of correct responses. If accuracy was significantly above the mean chance level of 33.33%, we inferred successful sleep-learning. Accuracy values of participants did not significantly deviate from a normal distribution at the 12 hr and at the 36 hr retrieval (pShapiro >0.148), variances did not significantly violate the assumption of homogeneity (pLevene >0.34), and all values were within the range of +/-2 standard deviations from the mean. We computed a 2x2 ANOVA with the between-subjects factor Peak versus Trough and the within-subjects factor Encoding-Test Delay (12 hr versus 36 hr). The dependent variable was retrieval accuracy expressed as the difference between the percentages of correctly retrieved associations minus the percentage of mean chance performance (33.33 %). A second ANOVA with the within-subjects factor Encoding-Test Delay (12 hr versus 36 hr) was computed for the Trough condition alone to determine whether the intercept is significant (indicating that the average retrieval accuracy exceeded chance level in the two encoding-test delays) and to determine whether retrieval performance was different at 12 hr versus 36 hr. Furthermore, we planned a comparison of retrieval performance against chance level at the 12 hr and at the 36 hr retrieval.

### EEG data analysis

#### EEG preprocessing

The raw EEG-data were re-referenced to the common average, band-pass filtered at 0.25–35 Hz, and down-sampled to 100 Hz. The continuous EEG data was subjected to manual artefact rejection. First, noisy channels and channels with strong sweat artefacts were visually identified and subsequently interpolated. Next, we visually identified and excluded data segments that contained muscle artefacts, movement artefacts, or arousals. Artefact rejection was performed by Flavio Schmidig, who was blinded to the participants’ condition (Peak/Trough) and to the type and timing of sound presentation.

#### Event-related EEG analyses

We computed sleep-recorded event-related potentials (ERPs) and event-related spectral perturbations (ERSPs) for each participant. For ERPs, we first epoched the raw EEG data into 7 s trials (from 3 s before to 4 s after word onset) and then averaged over all trials per condition and per participant. Moreover, we compared ERSPs between experimental conditions. To this aim, we computed the spectral power for the fast spindles (12–16 Hz) and the theta band (4–8 Hz). We estimated the power over the interval of 2 s before to 3 s after word onset using discrete wavelet transformation (20 ms steps, i.e. 50 Hz sampling rate). We used linearly increasing cycle numbers with 4.25 cycles at the lowest and 11.75 cycles at the highest frequency for the theta frequency band and with 4.25 cycles at the lowest and 11.75 cycles at the highest frequency for the spindle frequency band. ERSPs were baseline-corrected at the single trial level by normalising the time-series at each frequency using the frequency-specific mean and standard deviation of the power, which was computed across the entire trial (Grandchamp and Delorme, 2011). Baseline-corrected ERSPs were then averaged over all trials of a condition. This procedure was performed for each electrode, each condition, and each participant. Then, we computed the grand averages for the conditions (Peak condition, Trough condition, experimental condition, control condition, correct assignments in the experimental condition, incorrect assignments in the experimental condition). To test for statistical differences, we performed mass univariate analyses with cluster-based permutation statistics (1000 permutations) to correct for multiple comparisons (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007). Cluster-level Monte Carlo values were considered significant if error probability was lower than 5%.

#### Extraction of slow-wave characteristics

Our aim was to find out which slow-wave characteristics promoted sleep-learning. Therefore, we computed the standardized global field power of the targeted slow-wave (GFP, z-score) at the time of word onset in each trial. We averaged over the four presentations of a word pair and over each participant. Furthermore, we computed the Peak/Trough prototypicality, which reflected the similarity (Fisher’s z-transformed correlation values) between the electrical field (scalp maps) of the online-recorded EEG at word onset and the electrical field of the targeted slow-wave phase (Peak/Trough). Next, we extracted the inter-trial-phase coherence at word onset to estimate the consistency of the targeted slow-wave phase across the four presentations of each word pair (measured over frontal electrodes, a.u.). Finally, we computed the z-scored time delay between word onset and the time-point of the maximal amplitude of the targeted slow-wave peak/trough. We compared these parameters between correctly versus incorrectly assigned pseudowords at the 12 hr and the 36 hr retrieval. Where necessary, the data were z-transformed using Fisher’s transformation.

#### Offline detection of slow-wave peaks and troughs

In order to identify the delay between the time of word onset and the time of the maximal amplitude of the targeted slow-wave peak/trough, we post-hoc identified discrete slow-wave events in the EEG. Slow-waves were automatically detected by a MATLAB-based algorithm modelled after Mölle et al., 2002. Slow-wave peaks and troughs produce distinct brain wide voltage distributions (Ruch et al., 2014), which we used to target online slow-wave phases. For the off-line identification of slow-wave peaks and troughs, we used frontal derivatives. We bandpass-filtered the EEG from 0.5 to 1.5 Hz and averaged the EEG over the frontal electrodes ('F1', 'F2', 'F3', 'F4', 'Fz'). Next, we identified every zero-crossing in the bandpass filtered frontal signal. The local minima and maxima between zero-crossings were labelled as potential peaks and troughs. In this process, time and amplitude constraints were added. All slow-waves with durations shorter than 0.8 s or longer than 2 s were excluded. The resulting slow-waves lay between 0.5 and 1.25 Hz. A further criterion was slow-wave amplitude. The detected slow-wave half-waves needed to exhibit an amplitude (trough-to- peak) that exceeded two thirds of the slow-wave amplitudes per participant.

#### Estimation of neural complexity: Higuchi Fractal Dimension

We quantified the degree of information processing in the brain during and following word presentation during sleep. To this aim, we computed Higuchi Fractal Dimension (HFD) as an EEG-based measure of ‘complexity’ of ongoing neural activity. HFD provides a non-linear measure of the complexity, variability, and randomness of EEG time-series (Lau et al., 2022; Parbat and Chakraborty, 2021). Importantly, a high neural complexity has been associated with successful memory formation during wakefulness (Sheehan et al., 2018). We computed HFD separately for each trial and electrode for the EEG time-series of our windows of interest (see below) using the MATLAB code provided by Monge-Alvarez, 2024. Kmax for extracting HFD was set to 10 (Monge-Alvarez, 2024). Single-trial HFD values were averaged within participants separately for each condition (experimental condition and control condition), electrode, and time window of interest. Average HFD values were then used for group-level analyses.

We determined the degree of stimulus-induced information processing following word offset. To this aim, we computed HFD for the time window from 0.5 to 2 s following word onset. We used the HFD values, which were computed for the time window from –2 to –0.5 s before word onset, as a baseline in order to control for inter-individual differences in neural complexity. To test for statistical differences in HFD, we performed mass univariate analyses with cluster-based permutation statistics (1000 permutations) to correct for multiple comparisons (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007).

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.89601.3.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.89601.3.sa1)

The authors show that concurrently presenting foreign words and their translations during sleep leads to the ability to semantically categorize the foreign words above chance. Specifically, this procedure was successful when stimuli were delivered during slow oscillation troughs as opposed to peaks, which has been the focus of many recent investigations into the learning & memory functions of sleep. Finally, further analyses showed that larger and more prototypical slow oscillation troughs led to better categorization performance, which offers hints to others on how to improve or predict the efficacy of this intervention.

Comments on the revised version:

I applaud the authors on a nice rebuttal. Many responses use solid arguments based on the existing literature, such as their response regarding the possibility that low-level acoustic characteristics explaining EEG differences between conditions. Their new analyses also clarify the paper. Additionally, I appreciate their labeling their more speculative claims as such. Below are my remaining thoughts:

Major point:

The largest remaining issue for me regards the term 'episodic'. Before I begin, I should say that I imagine the authors have thought considerably about this definition and may disagree with what I will say. That would be fine - it's their choice at this journal. My main point in writing this is to help them clarify their case further. R3 had a similar concern on the first round of review, and I imagine others holding the "traditional" view of episodic memory would be similarly skeptical. If the authors have a great rebuttal to these points, I imagine it will address others' concerns too.

I believe I understand the authors' argument: I read the Henke (2010, Nature Reviews Neuroscience) piece years back with great interest and again now, and I've gone back to read their other papers cited in this manuscript. Again, I applaud the authors on producing a large collection of fascinating findings expanding knowledge of what can be accomplished via unconscious learning. That includes this paper! But I still disagree with the term 'episodic' for what is measured here. The authors state in the Methods section that they prompted participants to 'guess whether the presented pseudoword designates an animal, a tool, or a place'. IMHO, the main issue of using 'episodic' is the nature of the memory representation - 'guessing' does not ask participants anything about the source (the who-what-when-why-where) of the information (anything about an episode).

Notably, it does seem to fit their own definition from Henke (2010). Rapid? I believe so - 4 trial-learning is fairly quick. Certainly, there are studies of supposed episodic memory that use a few rounds of learning the same stimuli (rather than single trial learning) and one can still get away with calling the nature of the memories 'episodic'. Flexible? I believe the authors mean that their task is flexible because participants learn a category exemplar during sleep (e.g., 'aryl'-'bird') but then only respond based on its category membership ('animal'?). If this is the case, I agree that the representations are flexible. Reliant on the 'episodic memory system' (lines 495-9)? Reasonably likely, given their prior findings (e.g., Züst et al., 2019). However, there is considerable data suggesting the hippocampus contributes to functions beyond episodic memory, including statistical learning (e.g., Schapiro et al., 2013, Current Biology), motor learning (e.g., Schendan et al., 2003, Neuron; Dohring et al., 2017, Cortex; Jacobacci et al., 2020, PNAS), attention (e.g., Aly & Turk-Browne, 2016, Cerebral Cortex), perception (e.g., Lee et al., 2012), and semantic memory (e.g., Cutler et al., 2019, Frontiers in Human Neuroscience). Therefore, given that the hippocampus contributes to other tasks too, saying the task is episodic in part because it likely relies on the hippocampus (the 'episodic memory system') is an incorrect reverse inference. But regardless of this concern, it seems true to me that the term fits 'episodic' according to Henke (2010).

So, it seems I'm raising an issue with this entire way of defining memory. IMHO, the biggest issue is that there is no reason to assume the participant relies upon any source-related information in making their guess. There is room in the field for a new type of rapid, unconscious, flexible, hippocampal-dependent learning that does not need to align with the term, 'episodic', for it to be important and fascinating! The term, 'episodic', is convenient for a reason - namely, for labeling the behavioral output of what it measures, not the process that underlies it. The authors have continually made an excellent case for rapid, unconscious, flexible, hippocampal-dependent learning, and it would seem even more beneficial for the field for the authors to just call this its own thing.

A related point:

- I see that the authors do not use 'episodic' in prior papers with similar tasks (e.g., Züst et al., 2019), and I am curious if anything changed in their thinking or why they use the term now. They can ignore this if they'd like, but it would perhaps give useful context.

Other points:

IMHO, the issue of repeated tests is more legitimate than the authors suggest. They state in their response letter, "However, recent literature suggests that retrieval practice is only beneficial when corrective feedback is provided (Belardi et al., 2021; Metcalfe, 2017)." This is incorrect. While retrieval practice is often less effective without feedback, it can be effective without feedback if retrieval accuracy is high and if the experimenters later employ a long enough retention interval to witness long-term effects. This is clear in various papers (e.g., Roediger & Karpicke, 2006, Psychological Science; Karpicke & Roediger, 2008, Science) and there is a nice theoretical model explaining how these complex effects could arise (Halamish & Bjork, 2011, JEP:LMC; Kornell et al., 2011, JML). The authors do not heavily rely on this in their paper, but they could consider tempering their claims that it is 'unlikely' (line 509) that delayed retrieval was affected by the first retrieval.

The authors claim that fast spindles are part of a speculative model underlying their learning effects (lines 605-6). However, they did not find any differential spindle effects in determining later performance, so they could consider keeping just points #1&2 or mentioning that spindles differ by condition but may not directly influence the learning effects here.

This is a revision in response to the reviewer's comments. The authors provided new analyses and try to acknowledge limitations, overall doing a good job, but the interpretation still seems to me going above the available evidence, especially for the claim that it is episodic memory formation during sleep. I still believe the paper will be fairer in dropping this speculative part and omitting the word "episodic" from the title (like actually they did in the abstract). The argument of the authors is that they refer to a computational definition of episodic memory, which is to some extent valid, but I am afraid it is not the way it will be understood by most readers, and it will thus indirectly contribute to an erroneous (or at least, not substantiated) interpretation of the brain's sleeping capabilities.

My main concern is that I have not seen any proposal for a control condition allowing to exclude the alternative, simpler hypothesis that mere perceptual associations between two elements (foreign word and translation) have been created and stored during sleep (which, I repeat, is already in itself an interesting finding). The authors argue that it seems to them not an efficient processing, but this an opinion, not a demonstration.

results.result: Vocabulary presented during slow-wave troughs (but not peaks) led to above-chance retrieval performance at 36 hours post-encoding. Retrieval performance was significantly better in the Trough condition (39.11% correct, 5.77% above chance, p=0.032) compared to the Peak condition, with the effect most pronounced at 36 hours (p=0.036) rather than 12 hours (p=0.094).
results.evaluation: Claims C42, C45, and C47 provide converging statistical evidence with appropriate tests (ANOVA, planned contrasts) showing trough-targeted stimulation produces above-chance retrieval. The effect size (d=0.865) is substantial. However, the overall performance just failed significance (C41, p=0.077), and the 12hr vs 36hr difference was not significant (C43), suggesting the effect strengthens over time but with limited statistical power.

results.result: Item-level analysis revealed consistent category assignments across retrieval sessions (47% consistency vs. 33.3% chance) with no difference between conditions. In the Trough condition, participants showed higher rates of maintaining correct assignments (54% vs. 42% in Peak) and correcting initially incorrect assignments (32% vs. 27% in Peak).
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C51 provide descriptive evidence of memory stability and improvement over time in the Trough condition. The consistency rate exceeds chance level, and the pattern of maintaining/correcting assignments supports genuine learning. However, these are descriptive statistics without formal significance tests, limiting the strength of conclusions.

results.result: Encoding and retrieval occurred unconsciously during slow-wave sleep. Participants showed no conscious recognition of sleep-played pseudowords, as evidenced by feeling-of-having-heard (FoHH) ratings and confidence ratings that did not differ between sleep-played and new pseudowords, or between correct and incorrect assignments.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C58 provide multiple converging measures (FoHH, confidence ratings) showing no conscious awareness. The statistical tests (ANOVAs) consistently show non-significant differences (all p>0.1). The inference that encoding was unconscious (C53) is well-supported by the fact that stimuli were presented during slow-wave sleep (C52), which is characterized by loss of consciousness.

results.result: Successful encoding in the Trough condition was associated with a pronounced trough at stimulus onset. ERPs showed amplified voltage (larger frontal negativity and occipital positivity) for subsequently correct vs. incorrect assignments from -50ms to 260ms (p=0.016 frontal, p=0.010 occipital). The voltage distribution resembled a prototypical trough, and prototypicality significantly differentiated correct from incorrect assignments (p=0.005).
results.evaluation: Claims C68, C71, C73-C74 provide statistical evidence with cluster-based permutation tests showing that successful encoding requires a pronounced, prototypical trough. The effect is specific to the Trough condition (C69-C70 show no effects in Peak or between EC/CC). The prototypicality measure provides a quantitative link between trough characteristics and memory performance.

results.result: Trough-targeted word pairs (vs. pseudowords alone) enhanced theta power at 500ms (p=0.018) and fast spindle power at 1s (p=0.012) post-onset. Theta enhancement correlated significantly with retrieval performance (R=0.57, p=0.027), while spindle enhancement did not (R=0.034, p=0.9). These effects were absent in the Peak condition and did not differentiate correct from incorrect assignments.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 provide statistical evidence for spectral markers of encoding with appropriate cluster-based corrections. The correlation between theta and behavior (C78) supports a functional role, though the lack of trial-level differences (C80) suggests these are condition-level rather than item-level effects. The absence of spindle-behavior correlation (C79) is appropriately reported.

results.result: Neural complexity (HFD) was higher in the Trough than Peak condition post-stimulus (p=0.002). Word presentation reduced complexity in the Peak condition (p=0.002) but not in the Trough condition (p>0.1), suggesting differential processing. However, complexity did not differentiate correct from incorrect assignments or correlate with retrieval accuracy.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C89 show robust condition differences in neural complexity with appropriate statistics. The interpretation (C90, C95) that this reflects differential processing is reasonable but speculative. The lack of item-level effects (C92-C94) limits the functional interpretation, suggesting complexity reflects general processing state rather than specific encoding success.

results.result: Word-evoked potentials differed dramatically between conditions. Peak-targeted words evoked K-complex-like responses (early positivity at 200ms, large negativity at 550ms, late positivity at 900ms), while trough-targeted words evoked two positive frontal components (at 500ms and 1s). ERP differences vanished by 700ms, with comparable responses from 700ms-2s.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C67 and C125-C126 describe well-documented ERP patterns with appropriate citations. The K-complex identification (C62-C63) is supported by literature. The temporal dynamics are clearly described with specific latencies. This provides strong evidence for differential processing between conditions, though the functional interpretation requires additional support.

results.result: The authors propose a three-stage model of sleep learning: (1) vocabulary played during troughs passes the thalamic gate and undergoes perceptual/conceptual processing, raising neural complexity; (2) the following peak with increased theta power enables semantic-associative encoding; (3) a second peak with fast spindle power aids immediate consolidation, preparing for later consolidation stages resulting in successful 36hr retrieval.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C100 present an integrative model synthesizing the findings. While the model is consistent with the data (trough processing, theta at peaks, spindle power), it involves substantial speculation about mechanisms (C97-C99 use terms like "passed the thalamic gate," "provided conditions," "may have aided"). The temporal sequence is inferred rather than directly demonstrated, and alternative explanations are not fully excluded.

results.result: The authors propose that ongoing consolidation and sleep-protective responses during peaks inhibited psycholinguistic processing, while words were processed during troughs. They suggest psycholinguistic processing lasted ~500ms (matching word duration and trough duration), with parallel phonological, syntactic, lexical, and semantic analyses occurring during this window, similar to awake processing timelines.
results.evaluation: Claim C127 is an inference not directly tested. Claims C128-C129 are speculative about processing duration. Claims C130-C136 cite established knowledge about awake language processing but assume similar timing during sleep (C136), which is supported by limited citations. The model is plausible but lacks direct evidence for the proposed processing stages during sleep.

results.result: The authors propose that hippocampal encoding of pseudoword-translation associations occurred at 500ms post-onset, coinciding with theta power increase and a slow-wave peak. They suggest this timing reflects when semantic associations underwent hippocampal storage, supported by the peak providing necessary neuronal excitability and hippocampal-neocortical communication.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C139 cite established knowledge about hippocampal encoding and theta. Claim C140 reports the theta timing finding. However, claims C141-C143 are highly speculative interpretations ("might reflect," "may have contributed") without direct evidence of hippocampal involvement. The temporal coincidence is suggestive but not definitive proof of the proposed mechanism.

results.result: The authors propose that fast spindles at 1s post-onset supported immediate replay and consolidation of sleep-formed associations. They note spindle power increased in the experimental but not control condition, and both theta and spindle increases were accompanied by enhanced neuronal activity in the Trough but not Peak condition.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C146 cite established knowledge about spindle function. Claims C148-C150 report condition differences in spindle power and neuronal activity. However, claim C147 is speculative ("we assume"), and the lack of correlation between spindle power and behavior (C79) undermines the functional interpretation. The evidence is suggestive but not conclusive.

results.result: The authors propose a speculative three-step model of sleep learning: (1) troughs allow 500ms of language comprehension without K-complexes; (2) encoding occurs during the next peak at 500ms with enhanced theta; (3) fast spindles at 1000ms assist immediate replay. They acknowledge this model requires testing with MEG or simultaneous fMRI-EEG.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C154 present a detailed mechanistic model that integrates the findings but is explicitly speculative. Claim C155 appropriately acknowledges the need for future testing. The model is internally consistent with the data but involves substantial inference about unobserved processes (language comprehension stages, hippocampal encoding, replay). It serves as a hypothesis-generating framework rather than established fact.

results.result: The authors argue that the task requirements (rapid associative encoding, flexible retrieval) call upon the episodic memory system and hippocampus, not other memory systems. They cite evidence that only the hippocampus can rapidly form arbitrary associations in a flexible format, while the neocortex requires many trials. They reference a previous study showing hippocampal activation during retrieval of sleep-learned associations.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C104 cite established knowledge about hippocampal vs. neocortical learning. Claim C105 cites relevant prior work (Züst et al., 2019) using a similar task. Claim C106 provides a logical argument against priming explanations. Claims C101-C102 cite evidence for unconscious episodic memory. The argument is well-reasoned and supported, though direct hippocampal evidence in the current study would strengthen it.

results.result: Unlike typical episodic memories that decay rapidly over 24 hours, sleep-formed memories did not deteriorate from 12hr to 36hr and numerically strengthened. The authors speculate this may reflect additional sleep-dependent consolidation during the intervening night, with reactivation during the first test potentially tagging memories for further consolidation. They note that weak memories benefit especially from sleep consolidation.
results.evaluation: Claim C107 accurately describes the pattern (no significant decay, numerical increase). However, claims C108-C112 are speculative explanations without direct evidence. The lack of significant 12hr vs 36hr difference (C43) limits strong conclusions about strengthening. The speculation about tagging (C110) and preferential consolidation of weak memories (C111-C112) is plausible but unproven in this study.

results.result: The authors propose two explanations for why troughs but not peaks supported learning: (1) peaks may be occupied by consolidation of wake-formed memories, making them unreceptive to new learning; (2) targeting troughs bypasses sleep-protective K-complex responses that block processing during peaks. They cite evidence that peaks are associated with memory replay and spindles, while sounds during peaks evoke K-complexes that break down cortico-thalamic communication.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C120 are explicitly speculative ("may have been," "might therefore"). Claims C117-C118 and C121-C124 cite relevant literature about peak-associated consolidation and K-complexes. However, these are post-hoc explanations without direct evidence that peaks were "occupied" or that K-complexes specifically blocked learning. The explanations are plausible but require experimental testing.

results.result: The study included 30 participants (15 per condition) who were presented with an average of 23.98 word pairs during slow-wave sleep using a brain-state-dependent stimulation algorithm (TOPOSO). Pseudowords and translation words were simultaneously played to right and left ears respectively, with presentations lasting ~540ms and timed ~100ms before the targeted slow-wave phase maxima. Each word pair was presented four times in succession.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C40 and C177-C180 provide clear methodological details about the sample, stimulation parameters, and procedure. The description is sufficiently detailed for replication. The sample size (N=30, 15 per group) is modest but justified by prior work. The methodological choices (dichotic presentation, timing, repetitions) are clearly described and appropriately cited where relevant.

results.result: Sleep parameters differed between conditions: slow-wave sleep duration was significantly shorter in the Trough (26.3 min) than Peak (38.2 min) condition (p=0.01), and inter-stimulus interval was shorter in Trough (3.3s) than Peak (6.3s) condition (p<0.003). However, neither ISI nor slow-wave sleep duration correlated with retrieval accuracy at 36hr (both p>0.56), and the number of words played did not differ between conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C181-C188 report important methodological details and potential confounds. The statistical tests (C183-C186) are appropriate. The correlation analyses (C186) provide evidence that the group differences in sleep duration and ISI do not account for the behavioral effects, though this is based on absence of correlation rather than positive evidence. The inference (C187) is reasonable but not definitive.

results.result: The authors acknowledge three methodological limitations: (1) sound duration exceeded the targeted slow-wave phase duration, reducing specificity; (2) auditory complexity differed between experimental (word pairs) and control (single pseudoword) conditions, potentially inducing non-learning-related EEG differences; (3) carry-over effects from the first to second retrieval test may have contributed to the slight increase in accuracy.
results.evaluation: Claims C170-C172 appropriately acknowledge limitations that could affect interpretation. These are valid concerns: the stimulus duration issue (C170) affects the precision of phase-targeting; the complexity difference (C171) is a confound for EEG comparisons; and carry-over effects (C172) could inflate 36hr performance. The acknowledgment of these limitations is scientifically appropriate.

results.result: The authors compare the current study to their previous work (Züst et al., 2019) where words were played sequentially rather than simultaneously. They argue that in both studies, paired-associative encoding required a slow-wave peak (at ~500ms in the current study, during the second word in the prior study), because hippocampal encoding requires broadly activated neurons for effective hippocampal-neocortical connectivity. They note the prior study entrained the EEG, making the current study uniquely informative about endogenous slow-wave roles.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C163 provide appropriate comparison to prior work. The logic about timing differences (C157-C158) is sound. Claims C159-C161 cite relevant literature and make reasonable inferences about the necessity of peaks for encoding. Claim C163 appropriately distinguishes the current study's contribution. The comparison strengthens the interpretation of the current findings.

results.result: The authors argue that their findings of vocabulary acquisition during deep sleep, combined with evidence from subliminal learning during wakefulness, support the claim that episodic memory formation can proceed without conscious awareness. They argue the findings challenge views that slow-wave sleep involves general synaptic depotentiation, strict thalamic gating, and unidirectional (hippocampus-to-neocortex) information flow.
results.evaluation: Claims C164-C165 appropriately contextualize the findings within the broader literature on unconscious memory. Claim C166 accurately summarizes the behavioral pattern. Claims C167-C169 identify theoretical implications, though these are somewhat overstated—the findings challenge but do not definitively refute these views. The arguments are reasonable but would benefit from more nuanced discussion of alternative interpretations.

results.result: The authors discuss potential applications and ethical concerns of sleep-learning. They note sleep-learning might be exploited for nefarious purposes but could also be beneficial in psychotherapy, as sleep-learned messages circumvent conscious defense mechanisms and may allow modification of unwanted memories without conscious re-experiencing.
results.evaluation: Claims C173-C176 discuss speculative applications with appropriate citations. However, these are highly speculative extrapolations from the current findings. The study demonstrated only modest above-chance learning of arbitrary word pairs, which is far from the therapeutic applications suggested. The ethical concerns (C173) are valid but the practical applications (C174-C176) are premature given the limited effect sizes and lack of clinical evidence.

results.result: The study found that vocabulary presented during slow-wave troughs (but not peaks) led to above-chance semantic categorization performance at 36 hours post-encoding. Specifically, retrieval performance in the Trough condition was significantly better than the Peak condition (p=0.030), with performance 5.77% above chance at 36 hours (p=0.036).
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledge the findings as 'solid evidence' and 'valuable contribution' showing that trough-targeted stimulation leads to semantic categorization ability, multiple reviewers express fundamental concerns about the interpretation. One reviewer states the claim 'deviates from the typical use' of episodic memory terminology. Another reviewer emphasizes this could reflect 'mere perceptual associations' rather than episodic memory, calling for controls to exclude this 'simpler hypothesis.' The behavioral effect itself is accepted, but its theoretical interpretation remains contested.

results.result: The authors claim their findings demonstrate episodic memory formation during sleep, defined computationally as rapid, flexible, hippocampal-dependent associative learning that can occur without conscious awareness.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly challenge the use of 'episodic' terminology. One reviewer states 'the main issue of using episodic is the nature of the memory representation - guessing does not ask participants anything about the source...of the information (anything about an episode).' Another reviewer recommends 'omitting the word episodic from the title' and states the interpretation 'seems to me going above the available evidence.' A third notes the claim 'deviates from the typical use of this term in the literature.' Reviewers suggest the findings represent a distinct form of learning that should not be labeled 'episodic.'

results.result: The authors claim encoding and retrieval were unconscious because stimuli were presented during slow-wave sleep (accompanied by loss of consciousness) and participants showed no conscious recognition of sleep-played pseudowords on feeling-of-having-heard or confidence measures.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the unconscious nature of the learning. One reviewer explicitly states the manuscript 'supports the intriguing idea that some aspects of novel learning can occur during sleep and outside of awareness.' The evidence from feeling-of-having-heard measures and confidence ratings showing no difference between sleep-played and new items is not challenged by reviewers.

results.result: In the Trough condition, subsequently correctly assigned pseudowords showed amplified voltage (larger frontal negativity and occipital positivity) from -50 to 260 ms following word onset (p=0.016 frontal, p=0.010 occipital). The difference map resembled a prototypical trough, and trough prototypicality significantly differentiated correct from incorrect assignments (p=0.005).
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these EEG findings. One reviewer notes the authors 'showed that larger and more prototypical slow oscillation troughs led to better categorization performance, which offers hints to others on how to improve or predict the efficacy of this intervention.' The technical EEG analyses are accepted without critique.

results.result: Trough-targeted word pairs (versus pseudowords alone) enhanced theta power at 500 ms (p=0.018) and fast spindle power at 1 second (p=0.012) following word onset. Theta enhancement correlated with retrieval performance (R=0.57, p=0.027), while spindle enhancement did not (R=0.034, p=0.9).
results.evaluation: While reviewers do not directly challenge the spectral findings, one reviewer notes a logical inconsistency: 'The authors claim that fast spindles are part of a speculative model underlying their learning effects (lines 605-6). However, they did not find any differential spindle effects in determining later performance, so they could consider keeping just points #1&2 or mentioning that spindles differ by condition but may not directly influence the learning effects here.' This suggests the spindle findings' functional significance is questioned.

results.result: Baseline-corrected EEG complexity following word offset was higher in the Trough than Peak condition (p=0.002). Word pairs reduced post-stimulus complexity in the Peak condition (p=0.002) but not the Trough condition (p>0.1), suggesting word processing during sleep increases neural complexity in troughs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the neural complexity findings. One reviewer acknowledges the authors' 'new analyses also clarify the paper,' which included complexity analyses. The findings are presented as supporting evidence for differential processing between conditions and are not contested.

results.result: Words targeted to peaks evoked a K-complex-like generic response (early frontal positivity at 200 ms, large negative component at 550 ms, late positivity at 900 ms), while words targeted to troughs evoked two positive frontal components (at 500 ms and 1 second) that differed sharply from K-complexes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these ERP characterizations. One reviewer notes the authors provided 'solid arguments based on the existing literature, such as their response regarding the possibility that low-level acoustic characteristics explaining EEG differences between conditions,' suggesting the differential ERP patterns are accepted as valid.

results.result: Unlike typical episodic memories that decay rapidly, retrieval performance did not deteriorate from 12 to 36 hours. The authors speculate this reflects sleep-dependent consolidation during the intervening night, with weak memories particularly benefiting from consolidation, and reactivation during the first test tagging memories for reconsolidation.
results.evaluation: One reviewer explicitly challenges the authors' dismissal of repeated testing effects: 'IMHO, the issue of repeated tests is more legitimate than the authors suggest...retrieval practice...can be effective without feedback if retrieval accuracy is high and if the experimenters later employ a long enough retention interval.' The reviewer recommends 'tempering their claims that it is unlikely (line 509) that delayed retrieval was affected by the first retrieval.' The consolidation interpretation is questioned as potentially confounded.

results.result: The authors propose a three-stage speculative model: (1) troughs provide a 500 ms window for language comprehension without K-complexes; (2) at 500 ms, paired-associative encoding occurs during the next peak with enhanced theta power; (3) at 1000 ms, fast spindles assist immediate replay through hippocampal-neocortical interactions.
results.evaluation: One reviewer notes the authors 'appreciate their labeling their more speculative claims as such,' acknowledging the model's speculative nature. However, the same reviewer points out an inconsistency: 'they did not find any differential spindle effects in determining later performance, so they could consider keeping just points #1&2 or mentioning that spindles differ by condition but may not directly influence the learning effects here.' The model is accepted as speculation but with noted empirical gaps.

results.result: The authors argue that mere priming cannot account for the findings because priming is not compositional and flexible enough to support the cued retrieval of word meaning required by the task. They conclude translation words must have been understood and their meaning bound to pseudowords during sleep.
results.evaluation: One reviewer explicitly challenges this interpretation: 'My main concern is that I have not seen any proposal for a control condition allowing to exclude the alternative, simpler hypothesis that mere perceptual associations between two elements (foreign word and translation) have been created and stored during sleep (which, I repeat, is already in itself an interesting finding). The authors argue that it seems to them not an efficient processing, but this an opinion, not a demonstration.' The reviewer emphasizes the lack of empirical evidence to rule out simpler associative mechanisms.

results.result: The authors acknowledge a discrepancy in auditory complexity and information density between experimental (pseudoword-word pairs) and control (single pseudoword) conditions, which could induce processing and EEG differences beyond associative learning.
results.evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accept this limitation acknowledgment. One reviewer notes the authors provided 'solid arguments based on the existing literature, such as their response regarding the possibility that low-level acoustic characteristics explaining EEG differences between conditions,' suggesting this confound was discussed and the authors' response was deemed reasonable, though the limitation remains.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C52-C58. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers accept the evidence for unconscious learning during sleep, based on feeling-of-having-heard measures and confidence ratings showing no awareness of sleep-presented stimuli.

Both address behavioral findings (C42, C45-C47) showing trough-targeted stimulation produces above-chance retrieval. OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED with caveats about statistical power. Peer reviewers accept the behavioral effect as 'solid evidence' but rate UNCERTAIN due to fundamental concerns about whether this represents true episodic memory versus perceptual associations.

Both address EEG findings on prototypical troughs (C68, C71-C74). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED based on cluster-based permutation tests. Peer reviewers also accept these findings as SUPPORTED, noting they 'offer hints to others on how to improve or predict the efficacy of this intervention.'

Both address spectral markers (C76-C79). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED with note that spindle-behavior correlation is absent. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, specifically questioning the functional significance of spindles given the lack of differential effects on performance.

Both address ERP patterns (C60-C65, C125-C126). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting well-documented patterns with appropriate citations. Peer reviewers also accept as SUPPORTED, acknowledging the authors provided 'solid arguments based on existing literature.'

Both address neural complexity findings (C88-C89, C95). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED but notes interpretation is speculative and item-level effects are absent. Peer reviewers also rate SUPPORTED without challenging the complexity findings.

Both address memory consolidation over time (C107-C112). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting speculation about tagging and preferential consolidation lacks direct evidence. Peer reviewers also rate UNCERTAIN and explicitly challenge the dismissal of repeated testing effects as a confound.

Both address the integrative mechanistic model (C152-C154). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN, noting it's explicitly speculative and serves as hypothesis-generating framework. Peer reviewers rate UNCERTAIN, acknowledging the speculative labeling but noting empirical gaps, particularly regarding spindle effects.

Both address methodological limitations (C170-C171). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, noting appropriate acknowledgment of stimulus duration and complexity confounds. Peer reviewers implicitly accept as SUPPORTED, noting the authors provided solid arguments regarding these issues.

Both address episodic memory interpretation (C101-C103, C165, C22, C96). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED, accepting the episodic memory framework with citations. Peer reviewers rate UNSUPPORTED, explicitly challenging the 'episodic' terminology and recommending its removal from the title, arguing the evidence doesn't support this interpretation.

Both address arguments against simpler explanations (C106, C128). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED for the logical argument against priming. Peer reviewers rate UNSUPPORTED, explicitly stating this is 'an opinion, not a demonstration' and calling for control conditions to exclude perceptual association hypotheses.

Partial overlap on integrative model (C96). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN due to substantial speculation about mechanisms. Peer reviewers challenge the episodic memory interpretation more fundamentally, rating UNSUPPORTED and arguing the findings represent a distinct form of learning.

Minimal overlap (C128). OpenEval rates UNCERTAIN regarding processing duration assumptions during sleep. Peer reviewers focus on challenging simpler associative explanations, rating the episodic interpretation as UNSUPPORTED.

Minimal overlap (C165). OpenEval rates SUPPORTED for contextualization within unconscious memory literature, though notes theoretical implications are somewhat overstated. Peer reviewers fundamentally challenge the episodic memory framing, rating UNSUPPORTED.
